chapters.1: During a famine in Israel, Elimelech and his wife Naomi move to Moab with their two sons, who marry Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth. After Elimelech and both sons die, Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem. Orpah goes back to her own family, but Ruth refuses to leave Naomi, famously pledging to stay with her and her God no matter what. Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest, with Naomi feeling that God has dealt bitterly with her.
chapters.2: Ruth goes out to glean leftover grain in the fields to support herself and Naomi, and happens to end up in a field belonging to Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's late husband. Boaz notices Ruth, learns of her loyalty to Naomi, and shows her special kindness, telling his workers to let her gather extra grain safely. Ruth brings home an unusually large amount of barley, and Naomi recognizes that Boaz is one of their family's close relatives who could act as a kinsman-redeemer.
chapters.3: Naomi instructs Ruth to approach Boaz at the threshing floor at night, following a customary way of asking a kinsman to fulfill his duty toward a widow. Ruth uncovers Boaz's feet and lies down as instructed, and when he wakes, she asks him to act as her kinsman-redeemer. Boaz agrees in principle but explains there is another relative with a prior claim who must first be given the chance to redeem her and the family property. He sends Ruth home with a generous gift of barley and promises to resolve the matter the next day.
chapters.4: Boaz meets the nearer kinsman at the town gate before the elders and offers him the right to buy Naomi's land and marry Ruth; the man declines, so Boaz formally takes on the role himself, redeeming the property and marrying Ruth. The community blesses the marriage, and Ruth gives birth to a son named Obed. The book closes by tracing the family line from Obed to Jesse and then to David, placing Ruth the Moabite within the ancestry of Israel's great king.
